1:
This chapter, following what seemed the close of the Gospel (John 20:30–31), adds a further resurrection appearance. The grammatical-historical commentators identify the place as the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:18), where Jesus had promised to meet his disciples (Mark 14:28; Matthew 28:10). Robertson notes the verb “manifested himself” (ephanerōsen heauton), and that the risen Jesus was “only seen during the forty days now and then” (Acts 1:3), ten such instances being recorded. Augustine, for the Latin fathers, observes that “the preceding words seem to indicate the end of the book,” yet the Evangelist “goes on farther” to relate this appearance by the sea.

Calvin, for the Reformed, marks the purpose: the Evangelist “still labours to prove the resurrection of Christ,” relating that he “appeared to seven disciples,” whose testimony, given by men once slow to believe, is the more to be trusted. The witnesses thus find in the verse the opening of a further proof and a further lesson. The proof is the reality of the risen Christ, who shows himself yet again, bodily and unmistakably, to a company of his own; the resurrection rests not on a single sight but on repeated, varied appearances over forty days. The weight of the sentence lies in the manner — “on this wise shewed he himself” — for what follows is no mere apparition but a scene of teaching and restoration, in which the risen Lord meets his disciples at their old work, supplies their need, and recommissions the one who had denied him. The chapter that seems an appendix is, the witnesses observe, a precious record of the living Christ’s continuing care for his church.

The witnesses observe that this added chapter crowns the Gospel with a scene of grace. Having proved the resurrection by the appearances in the upper room, John records one more by the lake, where doctrine gives way to tender dealing — the risen Lord feeding his disciples and restoring his fallen apostle. The verse thus opens not a mere supplement but a fitting close, showing that the same Christ who rose in power stoops in love to provide for and recommission his own.
2:
Seven are gathered, and the list repays attention. The grammatical-historical commentators count seven disciples, of whom five are named: Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, and the two sons of Zebedee — who, Robertson observes, are James and John, “mentioned by name nowhere in John’s Gospel, apparently because John is the author.” The two unnamed, Lightfoot conjectures, were “probably Philip and Andrew.” Gill notes they were “together… in one house” in Galilee, not far from the sea and the mountain where Christ had appointed to meet them (Matthew 28:16). Barnes observes that, “while they were waiting for the promise of the Holy Spirit,” they “still found it proper to be usefully employed.”

The witnesses dwell on the little fellowship and its season. These were the days between the resurrection and Pentecost, the disciples gathered in Galilee, waiting upon the Lord’s further word and the promised Spirit. There is a fitness in the company: Peter, who had denied his Master and was soon to be restored; Thomas, who had doubted and now believed; Nathanael, the guileless Israelite (John 1:47); and John, the beloved disciple, who veils his own name and his brother’s under “the sons of Zebedee.” They are found together, in the bond of common discipleship, awaiting their Lord. The witnesses find here a quiet picture of the waiting church — not yet endued with power from on high, uncertain what their future service would be, yet keeping together and ready to be employed. It is to such a company, gathered and waiting, that the risen Christ comes; and the naming of the seven, by an eyewitness who was himself among them, sets the scene with the exactness of one who was there.

The company is named with an eyewitness’s precision, and that the mingling of the once-doubting and the once-denying with the faithful marks it as a true picture of the church. None of these men had earned the visit they were about to receive; they are simply found together, waiting and working, when the Lord drew near. The verse thus reminds the reader that Christ comes to his people not in their strength but in their waiting, and gathers the weak and the strong alike into one expectant fellowship.
3:
Peter returns to his old trade, and the nets come up empty. The grammatical-historical commentators read the proposal as natural and innocent: Peter “had been a fisherman by practice” (Robertson, noting the infinitive of purpose, halieuein), and in the interval before Pentecost returned to honest work. Ellicott insists it “does not express either an abandonment of their higher calling” or unbelief, but “the vivid representation by an ear-witness of what actually took place as they returned to their ordinary work.” Clarke suggests that “the scandal of the cross” had cut off the charitable support they had known (Luke 8:3), so they fell back on their nets. The fruitless night — “that night they caught nothing” — Barnes reads as ordered “in the providence of God, that the miracle which was wrought might appear more remarkable.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, judges that Peter’s fishing “ought not to be regarded as inconsistent with his office,” for though Christ had ordained him an Apostle, “he abstained from the exercise of the apostleship for a short time, till he should be clothed with new power.” The witnesses thus find in the verse both a homely realism and a providential design. The realism is the apostles at their nets — waiting men, filling the interval with familiar labour, neither presuming to begin their great work before the Spirit came nor sitting idle. The design is the empty net: their whole night’s toil takes nothing, that the morning’s miraculous catch might shine the brighter, and that they might learn afresh, before they were sent to be fishers of men, that without Christ they “can do nothing” (John 15:5). The preparation is a gentle one: the Lord lets them fail all night at their own craft, that he may meet them at dawn and fill their nets at his word.

The witnesses draw the practical lesson that honest labour is no betrayal of the higher calling. While they waited for the Spirit, the apostles did not despise common work; yet their fruitless night taught them that even at their own trade they could do nothing without their Lord. So the verse joins diligence and dependence: the disciple is to be busy in his calling, yet to learn afresh that the increase is Christ’s to give, and that the emptiest night may be the eve of the richest morning.
4:
Dawn brings him to the shore, and they do not know him. The grammatical-historical commentators picture the scene: Robertson reads the genitive absolute “when day was now breaking” (prōias ēdē ginomenēs), the dawn coming on while it was still dim; Jesus “stood on the shore” (John 20:19), appearing suddenly, “but no one knew whence or how” (Ellicott). The disciples “knew not that it was Jesus” — partly, Clarke and Barnes suggest, because of the twilight and the distance, partly, Wesley adds, because “their eyes were holden” (cf. Luke 24:16), as with the two on the Emmaus road. Gill finds comfort in the timing: “Christ visits his right early, and is a present help in time of trouble.”

The witnesses dwell on the tender providence of the scene. The Lord comes to his toiling, weary disciples at the breaking of day, after their fruitless night — standing on the shore, watching them, before they know him. The not-knowing is of a piece with the other resurrection appearances, where Christ is often unrecognised at first (Mary at the tomb, the two at Emmaus), the eyes of his own being held until he chooses to reveal himself. They find in it both a historical truth — the reality of a risen body, present yet not always at once known — and a spiritual lesson: that Christ is often near his people in their darkest, most fruitless hours, watching their toil, before they discern his presence. The disciples labour all night and catch nothing, not knowing that the Lord stands on the shore; and the witnesses bid the reader take heart, that the same Saviour stands near in every weary watch, ready to make himself known and to turn the empty night into a morning of abundance.

The witnesses find comfort in the picture of Christ standing unseen on the shore. He had watched their toil all night, as he sees his people in every dark and fruitless hour, though they know it not. The verse thus assures the weary believer that the Lord is never far in the time of failure, but waits, often unrecognised, to turn the empty net into an overflowing one. The morning that broke on the disheartened fishermen brought their risen Master with it.
5:
The address is tender and the question homely, and both repay notice. The grammatical-historical commentators note the word “Children” (paidia): Robertson calls it “a colloquial expression like ‘my boys,’” a diminutive of affection, used by Jesus here alone in addressing his disciples and adopted by the aged Apostle John in his Epistle (1 John 2:18). Clarke insists it means “little children, or beloved children,” a term “of familiarity and affectionate kindness,” and marvels how the margin made “Sirs” of it. The question, “have ye any meat?” — the word denoting what is eaten with bread, especially fish (Barnes) — is framed, Robertson notes, so as to expect the answer “No,” which they give.

The witnesses dwell on the gentleness and the purpose of the question. The risen Lord, still unrecognised, draws near with a word of affection — “Children” — and a homely inquiry after their success. The very tenderness of the address might have revealed him, as Lightfoot suggests, had their eyes not been held; it was a word they had often heard from his lips. The question, asked of one who knows the answer, is not for information but for instruction: it draws from them the confession of their failure — “No” — so that the empty net is owned before it is filled. The witnesses find here the way of Christ with his people: he comes near in love, leads them to acknowledge their own emptiness, and so prepares them to receive from his hand what their own labour could not win. The “No” of the weary fishermen is the necessary prelude to the great draught; and the affectionate “Children” of the unknown stranger is the first token that the One who stands on the shore is no stranger at all, but their loving Lord.

The witnesses dwell on the kindness of a question that seeks no information but an admission. Christ would have his disciples own their emptiness before he fills it, that the gift might be plainly his. So the affectionate ‘Children’ and the searching ‘have ye any meat?’ together prepare the way for the miracle: love draws near, failure is confessed, and the stage is set for the Lord to supply what their labour could not. The verse teaches that the honest ‘No’ of the helpless is the door to the abundance of Christ.
6:
A word from the shore fills the net, and the commentators dwell on the miraculous draught at Christ’s word. The grammatical-historical commentators note that Jesus, “willing to make himself known by a miracle, since they knew him not” (Gill), directs them to “the right side,” where “Jesus knew the fish were” (Robertson). The disciples, “being at a loss what to do, readily obey him, though they did not know who he was” (Calvin). The result is overwhelming: Robertson reads the imperfect “were not able to draw it” (ouketi ischyon) as “picturing the disciples tugging at the net,” which the multitude of fishes had filled. The scene closely echoes the earlier call by the same sea (Luke 5:6).

Wesley, for the Wesleyan, finds it more than a wonder of power: “not only a demonstration of the power of our Lord, but a kind supply for them and their families… and an emblem of the great success they should afterward have” in gathering men. Cyril of Jerusalem and others see in the draught a figure of the church’s ingathering by the Spirit. The witnesses thus find in the verse both a proof and a parable. As proof, it reveals the risen Christ, whose word commands the fish of the sea and fills in a moment the net that toiled all night in vain. As parable, it foreshadows the disciples’ coming work as “fishers of men”: cast where he bids, at his word, their labour — fruitless in their own strength — would gather a great multitude into the net of the gospel. A lesson is woven through it: the same toil that took nothing all night takes more than it can hold the moment it is done at Christ’s command; and so the church learns that all fruitful service flows from obedience to the word of her risen Lord.

The witnesses press the abiding principle the miracle enshrines. The net cast in their own wisdom took nothing; the same net, cast at his word, could not be drawn for the multitude. So the verse stands as a parable of all gospel labour: fruitfulness is not the reward of effort but the gift of obedience, and the servant who works at Christ’s command and in Christ’s strength will gather where his own striving failed. The toiling church is bidden to listen for the word from the shore.
7:
John knows him first and Peter reaches him first, and the commentators weigh both. Hearing that it was the Lord, Peter girt his fisher’s coat about him and cast himself into the sea.” The witnesses delight in the characteristic action of the two great apostles. The grammatical-historical commentators identify “that disciple whom Jesus loved” as John (John 13:23), and find in the scene “the traits of character which have before met us… exactly preserved” (Ellicott): John, “true to the life of contemplation, is first to trace” the Lord in the miracle and to say, “It is the Lord”; Peter, “true to the life of action,” is first to plunge toward him. Barnes notes John “was convinced by the apparent miracle”; Clarke explains the “fisher’s coat” (ependytēn, an upper garment) and that “naked” means only that Peter had been stripped of his outer coat for work (cf. 1 Samuel 19:24).

The witnesses dwell on the beautiful interplay of love’s two ways. John, the contemplative, perceives; Peter, the ardent, acts. The one knows the Lord by the eye of quiet discernment; the other, the moment he hears, cannot wait for the ship but girds himself and casts himself into the sea to reach his Master. There is tenderness in Peter’s haste: this is the man who had denied his Lord, yet, far from shrinking, he is the first to rush toward him — love outrunning shame, eager to be near the One he had wronged. They find here a lesson in the variety of grace: the same Spirit makes one disciple swift to discern and another swift to act, and the church needs both — the seeing of John and the going of Peter. And they note the providence in it, for Peter’s plunge toward the shore prepares for the searching, restoring conversation that the risen Lord is about to hold with him over the breakfast fire.

The witnesses find in the two apostles a lasting picture of the body of Christ, where differing graces serve one love. John’s quiet discernment and Peter’s headlong ardour are not rivals but partners; the church needs the eye that perceives the Lord and the heart that runs to him. And in Peter’s eager plunge, the witnesses read the surest sign of a love not quenched by his fall: the denier is the first to reach the shore, drawn by a grace that had already begun to heal him before ever the question ‘Lovest thou me?’ was asked.
8:
While Peter swam ahead, the other six brought in the catch. The grammatical-historical commentators note that they “came in the boat” — Ellicott prefers that to “little ship,” observing that the two Greek words are interchanged here as at John 6:17, and Robertson marks the diminutive form. The distance, “as it were two hundred cubits,” is about a hundred English yards; and Ellicott points out that the shortness of it “explains how they were able to drag the net in tow.” He adds a small stylistic datum: the Greek preposition used here with “cubits” is used of distance “only by St. John” (John 11:18; Revelation 14:20). The net, more exactly, came dragging “with the fishes” — the definite article pointing back to those with which it had just been filled (v.6).

Clarke reconstructs the method of fishing, and the detail makes sense of the scene. It was probably the kind “in which the net was stretched from the shore out into the sea”: those in the boat shot the net, “fetched a compass,” and brought in a hawser fastened to its other end, while those on shore “helped them to drag it in.” The net itself was weighted to the bottom and buoyed at the top “by corks, or pieces of light wood,” so that “all the fish that happened to come within the compass of the net were of course dragged to shore.” On such a method the catch depended wholly on where the net fell — which is Clarke’s point, for “the sovereign power of Christ had in this case miraculously collected the fish to that part where he ordered the disciples to cast the net.”

The verse carries a quiet contrast as well. Peter, all ardour, casts himself into the sea; the rest keep to their work and bring the draught to land, and both are forms of love, the impetuous and the steady. Gill notes that the boat was the same they had put out in. The exactness of the record — the boat, the cubits, the net too full to lift — reads as the sober memory of one who was there.
9:
The grammatical-historical commentators begin with the tenses. Ellicott notes that the original has them in the present, “describing the scene as it was impressed on the mind of the writer,” and Robertson agrees, calling “they see” a “vivid historical present.” Gill is careful that the landing was general: not only Peter but “all the rest of the disciples” came out of the ship and stood safe on shore. Robertson parses the going ashore by the verb used at Luke 5:2, and the fish as “lying as placed,” the participle giving the sense of something already set down — “so broiling with bread ready,” he adds: toast. The word for the fire of coals (anthrakian) is the one used at John 18:18, where Peter had warmed himself; Robertson pauses on it only to observe our own derivative, “anthracite.”

Ellicott raises a question of number that the English hides. The word rendered “fish” occurs in the singular here and at v.13 alone, so that the clause might be given “and a fish lying thereon, and a loaf”; yet “it seems clear that it may be collective, as our word ‘fish.’” He refers the term to its other occurrences in the chapter (v.10) and to the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:9, 11).

On where the meal came from the witnesses divide, and sharply. Clarke holds that it “appears to have been a new miracle.” His reasons are circumstantial: the fire cannot have been one the disciples kindled, “for it is remarked as something new”; they had caught nothing (v.5); and “here was a small fish upon the coals, and a loaf of bread provided to eat with it.” He concludes that “the whole appears to have been miraculously prepared by Christ.” Barnes declines the inference altogether. “We have no knowledge whence this was produced,” he writes — “whether it was, as Grotius supposes, by a miracle, or whether it was a place occupied by other fishermen, where they also might cook the fish which they had caught.” His rule of interpretation settles it for him: “as no miracle is mentioned, however, there is no reason for supposing that any existed in the case.” The two readings turn on nothing in the text itself but on what silence is taken to license.
10:
A meal was already waiting on the coals, yet the disciples are told to fetch some of their own catch. Ellicott takes the command as having been obeyed, and draws the modest conclusion that the fish they brought “furnished part of the meal of which they are about to partake.” Robertson notes only the grammar — the relative stands in the ablative by attraction, agreeing with the noun for fish — and adds the point that matters for the sense: “they had caught the fish by Christ’s direction” (v.6).

Calvin presses that direction into a lesson about ownership. “Though the net was filled in a moment, without any great labor on their part,” he observes, “yet the taking of them is not ascribed by Christ to the disciples” — the catch is spoken of as theirs, but the credit is not. He finds the same usage in the prayer for daily bread: “thus, we call the bread which we daily eat OUR bread, and yet, by asking that it may be given to us, we acknowledge that it proceeds from the blessing of God” (Matthew 6:11). What a man may rightly call his own he may still have to ask for.
11:
Peter hauls the net ashore, and the commentators dwell on the tally and the unbroken net. The grammatical-historical commentators note that Peter, at Christ’s command (Ellicott reads “therefore”), “went up” into the boat and “drew” the net ashore — doing now, Robertson observes, what the whole company had failed to do before (v.6). The number, “an hundred and fifty and three,” is given because it marked “a very unusual draught” (Barnes), the great fish actually counted; and the wonder is that, “for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.” Robertson notes the precise tally of these “large” fish.

Much has been made of the number 153, ancient and modern, the fathers and others finding in it various symbolic meanings, though the plain sense is simply the exact count of a remarkable catch, recorded by an eyewitness. More agree on the significance of the unbroken net: where the earlier draught had broken the nets (Luke 5:6), this net held, and many have read in it a figure of the gospel net that, however great the multitude it gathers, shall not break nor lose its catch. The witnesses thus find in the verse both the exactness of true testimony — the counted fish, the great size, the whole net — and a quiet emblem of the church’s ingathering. As the net brought every fish safe to land without breaking, so the gospel, cast at Christ’s word, would gather a great multitude of every kind and bring them safe to the shore of his kingdom, none lost, the net unbroken. Peter, soon to be made a fisher of men, draws to land the figure of his own coming work.

The witnesses add that the scene rewards Peter’s eagerness with a share in the work: he who first reached the shore now draws the net to land. The whole, in its exactness and its symbolism, has fed the church’s reflection for centuries. Yet the surest lesson is the plainest — that the net of the gospel, cast at the word of Christ, gathers a great and varied multitude and holds them fast, none slipping through, none lost, until all are brought safe to the feet of the Lord on the eternal shore.
12:
The invitation is gracious and the silence that meets it is awe-filled. The grammatical-historical commentators explain that “Come and dine” is properly “Come and break your fast” (aristēsate, Robertson), the early morning meal (v.4); Robertson pictures “a delightful breakfast of fresh broiled fish… with the hush of joyful surprise in the presence of the Lord.” The disciples “durst not ask, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord” — they were sure of his identity, yet held in a reverent silence, half-awe and half-wonder at the risen One in their midst.

Augustine, for the Latin fathers, observes that Christ did eat with them (as Luke records, Luke 24:43), “not to satisfy the wants of nature, but to show the reality of His resurrection” — though “the bodies of the just, when they rise again, shall need no food.” The Eastern Chrysostom makes the same point. Calvin, for the Reformed, asks what held the disciples from questioning, and finds it “shame arising from reverence” — not doubt, for they knew him, but a holy awe. The witnesses thus find in the verse a scene of tender majesty. The risen Lord plays the host at the lakeside breakfast, calling his weary fishermen to be fed; and they, certain it is he yet awed by the mystery of his risen presence, dare not break the silence with a question. The blend of intimacy and reverence that marks all true communion with Christ: near enough to share his table, yet bowed in wonder before the One who has conquered death and now breaks bread with his own.

The witnesses dwell on the union of nearness and awe in this breakfast. The disciples sit at the Lord’s table, yet none dares speak a needless word; they are his friends, and yet they tremble before the mystery of his risen life. So the verse models the spirit of all true worship, which draws near with confidence and bows with reverence. To know that it is the Lord is at once to be at home in his presence and silenced by his glory; and the lakeside meal becomes a quiet sacrament of communion with the living Christ.
13:
The risen Lord acts as host at his own fire. The grammatical-historical commentators picture the scene with the vivid presents (Robertson): Jesus “taketh the bread, and giveth them,” serving his disciples “as host at this early breakfast, his last recorded meal with these seven faithful followers.” Gill describes him taking “his place as the master of the feast, and head of the family,” distributing the bread and fish. Clarke notes that he ate with them as well (Luke 24:43). Ellicott and others hear in the taking and giving of bread an echo of the Last Supper (cf. John 20:22; Luke 24:30).

The witnesses dwell on the gentle grace of the act. The same hands that had been pierced now take the bread and give it to his own; the Lord of glory serves breakfast to his fishermen. The gesture would have stirred their memory — of the feeding of the multitudes, when he took bread and gave (John 6:11), and of the upper room, where he broke bread the night before he died, and of Emmaus, where he was known “in breaking of bread.” In this familiar act the risen Christ both confirms that it is truly he and shows that his love and his lowly service are unchanged by his rising. The witnesses thus find in the verse a precious picture of fellowship restored: the disciples, scattered by his death, are gathered again at his table, fed by his hand, in quiet communion with their living Lord. The One who conquered death stoops to give them bread and fish — the risen Saviour still the servant of his people, still the host who spreads the table and bids them eat.

The witnesses find the deepest comfort in the constancy the gesture reveals. Resurrection has not changed the heart of Christ: the hands that broke bread in the upper room break it again on the shore, and the Lord who washed his disciples’ feet now serves them breakfast. So the verse assures the believer that the risen and reigning Saviour is the same who stooped to feed and serve, and that his exaltation has not lifted him above the lowly love that ministers to his own. He is the host of his people still.
14:
The reckoning is a careful one, and the grammatical-historical commentators are at pains to say what it counts. Robertson supplies the implied phrase, “to the disciples” — this is the third manifestation to them as a body. Clarke numbers those three precisely: Christ appeared to ten of them (John 20:19), again to eleven (John 20:26), and now to the seven named at the opening of this chapter (v.2). Gill reads the count the same way and states the qualification that makes it true: within that compass of time Christ “had made more appearances than three, though to particular persons, and not to such a number of the disciples as at these three times.” Ellicott puts it as an omission on the Evangelist’s part — he “passes over… the appearances to Mary Magdalene and others.”

Clarke then collates the other evangelists, and the number changes. Counted that way, this was the seventh manifestation after the resurrection: to Mary of Magdala (Mark 16:9); to the holy women who came from the tomb (Matthew 28:9); to the two who went to Emmaus (Luke 24:13); to Peter alone (Luke 24:34); to the ten in Thomas’s absence; eight days later to the eleven with Thomas present; and now to the seven, “which was between the eighth and fortieth day after his resurrection.” Beyond these he reckons an eighth, to the disciples on a mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:16); a ninth, if it be distinct from that one, to the five hundred brethren at once (1 Corinthians 15:6); a tenth, to James (1 Corinthians 15:7); and an eleventh, to all the apostles at Bethany when he ascended in their presence (Luke 24:50–53; Acts 1:3). He adds the honest caveat that “there might have been many other manifestations, which the evangelists have not thought proper to enumerate, as not being connected with any thing of singular weight or importance.”

Calvin explains why a day’s events count as one showing: “the number refers to the distance of time,” so that all transacted on a single day is included in one manifestation, and the appearances were spaced at intervals in order to confirm the disciples. Wesley reads the ordinal in the same restricted sense, of the times Christ appeared to so many of them together. Augustine, for the Latin fathers, notes what the verse does for the book: with this third manifestation “the Gospel of the blessed Apostle John is brought to a close.”
15:
The address is formal, and the grammatical-historical commentators note that the better text gives “Simon, son of John,” the name Peter bore before his calling. Robertson takes “these” as an ablative of comparison referring to the other disciples, and recalls that Peter “had even boasted that he would stand by Christ though all men forsook him” (Mark 14:29). He admits a gap in the record — “we do not know what passed between Jesus and Peter when Jesus first appeared to him” (Luke 24:34) — but of the purpose here he is confident: “Christ probes the inmost recesses of Peter’s heart to secure the humility necessary for service.” Barnes allows that “these” is slightly ambiguous, and may point either to the boats and nets at hand or to the men standing by.

Lightfoot presses the comparative itself. “Why more than these? Might it not have been enough to have said, as well as these?” — and he presses it hardest against the one disciple it would seem to slight, “especially more than St. John, whom Christ himself had so loved, and who had stuck so close to him?” He concludes that Christ “seems, therefore, to reflect upon Peter’s late confidence, not without some kind of severity and reproof,” and renders the force as direct speech: Peter had professed “beyond all the rest” that he would rather die than deny — “what sayest thou now, Simon? Dost thou yet love me more than these?” Clarke reads the design of the whole exchange in the same key: Peter “had thrice denied his Lord, and now Christ gives him an opportunity… to repair his fault by a triple confession.”

The answer is quieter than the question, and Robertson shows how. “Peter makes no claim here to superior love and passes by the ‘more than these,’ and does not even use Christ’s word agapaō for high and devoted love, but the humbler word phileō for love as a friend.” What he does insist on is that Christ knows it “in spite of his conduct.” The charge that follows uses a herdsman’s word (boskō, to feed as one pasturing a flock), and the objects of it are named by a diminutive — arnia, little lambs.

Chrysostom, for the Eastern fathers, makes the exchange turn on a general principle: of all the things that give boldness towards God, “that which most of all brings good will from on high, is tender care for our neighbor. Which therefore Christ requireth of Peter.” He answers too the question why Peter and not the rest — “he was the chosen one of the Apostles, the mouth of the disciples, the leader of the band,” so that even Paul “went up upon a time to enquire of him rather than the others.” And he marks what Christ does not do: “he bringeth not forward the denial, nor reproacheth him with what had taken place,” but puts the charge as an appeal — “if thou lovest Me, preside over thy brethren, and the warm love which thou didst ever manifest, and in which thou didst rejoice, show thou now; and the life which thou saidst thou wouldest lay down for Me, now give for My sheep.” Theophylact notes that the superintendence of the flock is thereby committed to Peter, and Augustine, for the Latin fathers, that Christ asked what he already knew, for Peter’s own good. Calvin adds that Peter is here “restored to that rank of honour from which he had fallen,” his denial having rendered him unworthy of the apostleship. Lightfoot ventures a conjecture on the threefold charge, applying the repeated “Feed” to the threefold object of Peter’s ministry — the Gentiles, the Jews, and the Israelites of the ten tribes.
16:
The question comes a second time, Gill says, because Christ was “willing to have the expressions of his love repeated and confirmed.” Ellicott notes that it is repeated “in exactly the same form, except that our Lord does not continue the comparison ‘more than these.’” Robertson makes the same observation from the Greek: Jesus “drops the pleon toutōn and challenges Peter’s own statement,” and “Peter repeats the same words in reply.” The pressure is now on the love itself rather than on any pre-eminence claimed for it.

The charge, however, changes its verb. Robertson gives it as poimaine, a present imperative from the noun for shepherd, so that the sense is “shepherd my sheep” rather than simply feed them — and the object is again a diminutive, probatia, little sheep. Barnes draws out what the change of word carries: unlike the verb of the previous verse, this one “has the sense of governing, caring for, guiding, protecting — the kind of faithful vigilance which a shepherd uses to guide his flock, and to make provision against their wants and dangers.” He finds a distinction of persons implied in it as well: “the care needed for the young in the church is to instruct them, and for those in advanced years both to instruct and govern them.” And where the first charge named the lambs, “my sheep,” he says, “commonly denotes the church in general, without respect to age” — the flock of John 10, to which he refers the reader, with the Great Shepherd of Hebrews 13:20 and the Shepherd and Bishop of souls of 1 Peter 2:25.

Calvin is careful about whose sheep they are, and the limit is deliberate. Christ “does not give to Peter and others the office of feeding all sorts of persons,” but commits to them his own — those who “hear my voice, and follow me” and who “hear not the voice of a stranger” (John 10:27; John 10:5). The commission is therefore not a general licence over men but a trust over a flock that remains Christ’s, recognisable by its hearing of his voice; and the shepherd set over it holds it on those terms.

Calvin will not let the limit become an excuse for narrowness, and the balance he strikes is careful. Faithful teachers “ought to endeavor to gather all to Christ”; since they cannot tell the sheep from the wild beasts, “they ought to try by all methods if they can tame those who resemble wolves” instead. Yet after their utmost efforts, he holds, “their labor will be of no avail to any but the elect,” because docility and faith arise from the Father delivering to his Son those “whom he elected before the creation of the world.” None come to salvation by the gospel “but those who are mild and teachable” — and then Calvin turns the point round, lest the mildness be mistaken for a natural endowment: “it must also be observed, that the Spirit of God tames those who by nature were bears or lions.”
17:
The third asking answers the threefold denial, and Barnes reads it as discipline and commission together: Christ “tenderly admonished him of his fault… while he solemnly charged him to be faithful.” Ellicott feels the force of the repetition from Peter’s side. This time “the Lord uses Peter’s own word,” so that the question “seems to say, ‘Dost thou, in personal affection and devotion, really love Me?’” — and he lets the exclamation stand: “the third time, to him who had three times denied! and this time the love which Peter knows has ever filled his soul seems to be doubted. The question cuts to the very quick.”

Robertson states the verbal point with more precision than it is usually given. In the first two questions Jesus had used agapaō, and Peter had answered with phileō; now “Jesus picks up the word phileō used by Peter and challenges that.” On whether the interchange is meaningful at all Robertson grants the general case and holds the particular one: “these two words are often interchanged in the N.T., but here the distinction is preserved.” Peter “was cut to the heart” — the verb is elypēthē, to grieve — because the challenge fell on that very word; and Robertson adds that “no doubt the third question vividly reminds him of the three denials in the early morning by the fire.” Clarke reports Chrysostom’s suggestion that Peter feared Christ saw in his heart something he did not see himself. Hence the appeal, in Ellicott’s words “in more emphatic words than before to the all-seeing eye that could read the very inmost secrets of his life”: “Lord, Thou knowest all things; Thou knowest that I love Thee.”

The nouns raise a textual question which Ellicott works through at length. He judges the better reading here to be “little sheep,” the difference from “sheep” amounting to a single letter, which a copyist might easily mistake. The diminutive occurs nowhere else in Biblical Greek and is therefore almost certainly original; whether it stood first here or at v.16, or in both, he leaves undetermined. The Received text runs lambs, sheep, sheep. The Peshito Syriac must have read lambs, little sheep, sheep — supported in part by the Vulgate, and “more exactly by the Latin of St. Ambrose, who has agnos, oviculas, oves.” That sequence “would point to a three-fold gradation answering to the three-fold question.” Yet Ellicott declines it: “it must be admitted that the more probable reading is lambs, little sheep, little sheep, and that the difference of thought is in the difference of the verbs” — “feed My lambs; be a shepherd to the weak ones of the flock; feed these weak ones.” Robertson records the same variation, noting that many manuscripts read “sheep” for “little sheep” both here and at the previous verse.

Calvin observes that Peter “undoubtedly did not perceive the object which Christ had in view” in pressing the same question so often, and took himself to be indirectly accused. Ellicott draws the charge out into the pastoral office. The man who had been loved and forgiven, held up that he might not fall and restored after falling, “is to be to others what Christ had been to him” — feeding men with spiritual truths as they can bear them, and guiding gently those who are weak through ignorance, prejudice or waywardness. He closes with an observation worth the whole discussion: as “a remarkable instance of how the Great Shepherd’s words impressed themselves upon the Apostle’s mind,” compare Peter’s own description of Christ as the Shepherd and Bishop of souls (1 Peter 2:25).
18:
Under the formula of solemn asseveration Christ foretells how Peter will die. The grammatical-historical commentators read the contrast of youth and age (Robertson noting the imperfects of customary action): in his vigour Peter “did as he pleased — he girded himself” and went where he would (Barnes); but in age he would “stretch forth his hands” and be girded and carried by another “whither he would not.” Clarke and Wesley find in “stretch forth thy hands” and being “girded” and “carried” a plain description of crucifixion — the Roman custom of binding the condemned to the cross, the hands outstretched. The Eastern Chrysostom reads the whole as Christ informing Peter “of his future martyrdom… an intimation to us how we should love.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, finds Christ here arming Peter “to maintain the warfare which was approaching,” demanding “not only faithfulness and diligence, but invincible courage in the midst of dangers, and firmness in bearing the cross.” The witnesses thus find in the verse a solemn honour conferred on the restored apostle. The man who once, to save his life, denied his Lord is told that he will one day lay down his life for him — the threefold denier made, by grace, a martyr. Tenderness and cost are held together here: Christ does not hide from Peter the hard end of his discipleship, but foretells the cross that awaits him, “whither thou wouldest not,” for nature shrinks from death even where love will embrace it. The prophecy, the witnesses observe, both seals Peter’s restoration — he who denied will be faithful unto death — and sets before every disciple the truth that to follow Christ is to take up the cross, and that the love which feeds his sheep may be called at last to die for his name.

The witnesses observe the perfect reversal grace has wrought. The Peter who girded himself and went where he would, who in his self-confidence followed afar and denied, will in his age be girded by another and carried where nature would not go — and will glorify God in it. The verse thus shows that the love now restored will be proved to the uttermost; the disciple healed of his denial will not deny again, but will stretch out his hands upon a cross. What he could not do in his own strength he will do by the grace that made him faithful unto death.
19:
The parenthesis is the Evangelist’s own. Ellicott recognises it as “a comment by the writer, and quite in St. John’s style,” comparing the similar asides elsewhere in the Gospel (John 12:33; John 18:32), and enters a careful qualification: the phrase “indicates generally the martyrdom of Peter as distinct from a natural death, without special reference to the crucifixion.” Barnes reads the foretold death as one “such as to honour God.” Ellicott adds that from its use here of Peter the phrase “glorify God” “passed into the common language of the Church for the death of martyrs” (compare 1 Peter 4:16). Clarke and Robertson report the ancient tradition that Peter was crucified at Rome some thirty-four years afterwards, and “deemed it so glorious a thing to die for Christ that he begged to be crucified with his head downwards,” holding himself unworthy to die as his Master had.

On the command itself Ellicott allows a plain surface meaning — that Christ withdrew a little and signalled Peter to come after him — but insists the words “must have had for the Apostle a much fuller meaning,” and traces why. By that same lake Peter “had first heard the command ‘Follow Me’” (Matthew 4:19); when sent out on his apostleship he had been taught that following Christ meant taking up the cross (Matthew 10:38); it was his own words that drew out the saying about denying oneself and taking up one’s cross; and to his question at the Last Supper came the answer, “Whither I go, thou canst not follow Me now; but thou shalt follow Me afterwards” (John 13:36). Now the command returns with a prophecy of martyrdom attached, and must have carried “the thought that he was to follow the Lord in suffering and death itself, and through the dark path which He had trodden was to follow Him to the Father’s home.”

Augustine does not treat the singling out of Peter as settled. He calls it “no unimportant question why the Lord… said unto the Apostle Peter, ‘Follow me,’ but of the Apostle John, ‘Thus I wish him to remain till I come,’” and devotes his last discourse on the Gospel to it. His difficulty is twofold. The others present followed Christ as their Master no less — “why is it said to Peter, ‘Follow me,’ and not to the others who were likewise present?” And if the words bear only on suffering, “was Peter the only one that suffered for the truth of Christianity?” He points to the company itself for the counter-instance: among those seven stood the other son of Zebedee, John’s brother, who after the ascension “is plainly recorded to have been slain.”

Calvin takes the circumlocution as “highly emphatic.” Every believer ought to glorify God by life and death alike, yet John means “a remarkable commendation for adorning the death of those who, by their blood, seal the Gospel of Christ and glorify his name.” He turns it to use — it is our own indolence “if our faith be not confirmed by it” — and then against what he calls “that sacrilegious and detestable invention… that their death contributes to appease the wrath of God.” Of the prediction’s purpose he is specific: it was “that Peter might be prepared to endure it; as if he had said, Since you must endure death by my example, follow your leader.” The point is narrower than imitation in general, since Christ “speaks only of the kind of death” — and it carries its own comfort, for what “greatly soothes all the bitterness that is in death” is that the Son of God “presents himself before our eyes with his blessed resurrection, which is our triumph over death.” Wesley sums the lesson: “it is not only by acting, but chiefly by suffering, that the saints glorify God.”
20:
Peter, walking after Christ, turns and sees John following too. The grammatical-historical commentators picture the scene: Peter, rising to follow Christ (v.19), “turning about” (epistrapheis, Robertson’s sudden turn), sees John “following” at a distance — the beloved disciple, identified again by his place at the supper (John 13:25), naturally drawn to keep near his Lord and his friend Peter (Ellicott). Henry notes Peter “in obedience to his Master’s orders, followed him, and turning about” saw John behind.

The witnesses dwell on the natural human touch of the moment and its preparation for what follows. John, “more than any other,” had been the companion of Peter (Ellicott); the two are often together in the Gospels and the Acts. As Peter is called to follow Christ to a martyr’s death, he turns and sees the beloved disciple following too, and his thought goes at once to his friend’s future. The Evangelist’s self-identification is a modest one — naming himself only as “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who had leaned on his breast — so that the reader knows who is meant without his ever claiming the honour. The verse thus sets the stage for Peter’s question about John (v.21) and the Lord’s answer about each disciple’s distinct path. The witnesses find in it a gentle reminder that the followers of Christ, bound in love to one another, are yet each given their own way to follow him — and that Peter, just charged to mind his own discipleship, must learn not to be over-curious about his brother’s.

There is a quiet artistry in naming himself only in love’s terms — the disciple Jesus loved, who leaned on his breast. He claims no rank but the Master’s affection. And they observe how naturally the scene unfolds: Peter, his own future just disclosed, turns to his lifelong friend, and his thought runs to John’s lot as well. The verse thus prepares, with the truthfulness of memory, for the lesson the Lord is about to teach — that each disciple has his own appointed path, and must follow Christ without comparing his portion to another’s.
21:
Peter’s question is about someone else’s future. The grammatical-historical commentators read the abrupt question — Robertson renders the Greek literally, “But this one… what?” (houtos de ti?) — as prompted, most agree, by “loving interest in the future of his friend” (Ellicott). Having just heard his own end foretold (vv.18–19), Peter turns to the beloved disciple following behind and asks what shall become of him. Gill reads John’s rising and following as itself significant, taking Peter to have understood it as a sign of his readiness “for service and suffering in the cause of Christ.” Barnes takes the question to mean “What death shall he die?”, Peter perhaps wondering whether John, the favoured disciple, should “have a happier lot.”

The witnesses dwell on the mingled good and ill in Peter’s question. There is affection in it — the natural concern of one friend for another, the two having shared the dark days and talked together of their Master’s words. But there is also a touch of the curiosity that looks aside from its own path to inquire into another’s. Peter has just been told to “follow me,” and his first impulse is to ask about John. The witnesses find here a very human moment, true to Peter’s warm and impulsive character, and the occasion of the Lord’s gentle correction to come. They observe that the question, though springing partly from love, needed the reproof Christ would give: the disciple charged with his own great calling and his own cross must not be over-busy about his brother’s lot, but must keep his eye on his Master and his own way of following him.

Peter’s question is the very thing the Lord must correct. Scarcely commissioned and called afresh to follow, he is already glancing at his brother’s portion. The verse thus catches the perennial temptation of the disciple — to measure his own lot against another’s, to wonder why one is called to suffer and another spared. And it sets the stage for a word that has steadied the church ever since: that each servant has his own appointed way, and the business of every follower is not comparison but obedience.
22:
The reply rebukes the curiosity and renews the call in one breath. The grammatical-historical commentators note the conditional form — Robertson reads “if I will” (ean thelō, third class) and “while I am coming” (heōs erchomai) — and the “sharp rebuke to Peter’s curiosity” in “what is that to thee?” Christ does not say John will tarry, but only, “If I will it, what concern is that of yours?” On “till I come,” the commentators offer several senses: the destruction of Jerusalem (Wesley — “he did tarry till Christ came to destroy Jerusalem”), the day of judgment, or simply that John should not die a violent death like Peter. The emphatic close turns Peter back to his duty: “follow thou me” — mind thine own discipleship.

Calvin, for the Reformed, is careful that the former clause not be read as a flat assertion that John would not die — a mistake, he notes, that arose by a slip of transcribers — for Christ speaks hypothetically. The witnesses thus find in the verse a word for every disciple tempted to compare his lot with another’s. Christ asserts his sovereign right to dispose of each of his servants as he wills — one to a martyr’s cross, another to a long life and a quiet end — and bids Peter not to question that disposal but to attend to his own following. The emphasis falls on the pronoun: “follow thou me,” whatever I appoint for him. The lesson, they find, is that the path of discipleship is personal and varied: each is given his own way to glorify God, and the believer’s business is not to scrutinise his brother’s calling but to be faithful in his own. Curiosity about another’s portion is rebuked; obedience in one’s own is commanded.

The witnesses press the largeness of the principle. Christ claims for himself the sovereign right to appoint to each of his servants a different path — one a swift martyrdom, another a long and quiet labour — and forbids the disciple to dispute or even to inquire into that disposal. The verse thus comforts and rebukes at once: it comforts, that our lot is in his wise and loving hand; it rebukes the restless curiosity that would compare callings. ‘Follow thou me’ is the whole of duty, whatever he wills for another.
23:
A rumour had grown out of the saying, and the Evangelist stops to correct it. Barnes finds the mistake natural on two counts: the words themselves “might be easily misunderstood to mean that he should not die,” and the impression was probably confirmed as John outlived all the other apostles, escaped the dangers of persecution, and settled to “a peaceful life at Ephesus.” The correction, Barnes adds, he thought proper to make before he died, leaving on record both what Jesus said and what he meant. Robertson puts the apostle’s motive plainly — he “is anxious to set this right” — since Jesus “was rebuking Peter’s curiosity, not affirming that John would live on till the Master returned.”

Ellicott locates the error precisely in a point of grammar. It “arose from their not attending to the force of the conditional particle”: they “took as a statement what had been said as a supposition,” and read it in the light of “the then current belief that the Second Advent would come in their own generation” (compare 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; 1 Thessalonians 4:17). He notes too that “brethren” as a general name for the disciples “is not elsewhere found in the Gospels,” and finds the key to it in Christ’s own words to Mary Magdalene (John 20:17) — a point Wesley makes as well. Ellicott then turns the whole episode into evidence: the mistake and its correction “are both interesting in their bearing upon the date of the Gospel,” and furnish “that kind of evidence which is perfectly natural as a growth, but which cannot possibly be made.” An inventor would not have thought to plant a correction of a rumour about himself.

Calvin identifies the brethren among whom it spread as those present at the conversation, the apostles — “the first-fruits, as it were, of that holy union” — and perhaps others then in their company; the error travelled “in all directions,” though probably not for long, lasting only until, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, they “formed purer and more correct views of the kingdom of Christ, having laid aside carnal and foolish imaginations.”

From this Calvin draws a general warning, and makes the apostles the argument for it. What John records happens every day, he says, and is no cause for wonder: if disciples who belonged to Christ’s own family and were intimately acquainted with him could be “so egregiously mistaken,” how much more those “who have not been so familiarly instructed in the school of Christ?” The fault, he insists, is never in the teaching: “the teaching of Christ is useful, and for edification; that is, it is plain; but we obscure the light by our wicked inventions, which we bring to it from our own views.” Christ had meant only to affirm his full power to decide about John’s life and death, while the disciples “imagine and contrive more than had been told them.” His diagnosis is blunt — “such is the wantonness of the human understanding, that it rushes with all its force into foolishness” — and he can point to the proof, since the rumour outlived the warning written against it: “a fable has been contrived, that he ordered a ditch to be digged for him, and went down into it, and that next day it was found empty.” Hence his conclusion: “we shall never cease to err, unless we unreservedly receive what the Lord hath taught us, and reject all inventions of men.”
24:
The verse is a formal attestation, and Ellicott places it structurally: as John 20:30–31 closed what seems to have been the original Gospel, so this closes the epilogue — though the words are “too wide to be limited” to it and “clearly refer to all that has preceded.” They identify the writer with the disciple just named, and imply that he “was still living, and bearing witness to their truth.” Robertson finds in it “a definite statement that the Beloved Disciple wrote this book,” and Calvin notes that John, having till now spoken of himself in the third person, “now declares that it is himself, that greater weight may be attached to the statements of one who was an eyewitness.”

The plural “we know” is the difficulty, and the witnesses take three distinct routes through it. Clarke thinks “it is very likely that these two verses were added by some of the believers at that time, as a testimony to the truth of the preceding narration” — probably “by those to whom John gave his work in charge.” Bishop Pearce and others, he records, hold instead that John means himself, but he judges that “very unlikely.” He dismisses a conjectural repointing of the Greek into “I know indeed” as “mere conjecture, and worthy of no regard,” and is careful that the Gospel loses nothing either way: it “loses no part of its authority in admitting the suffrage of the Church of God.”

Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by a different road, and closes off the usual defence on the way. “Our first and natural thought is that these are not the words of the writer of the Gospel, but the additional witness of persons knowing him.” It is customary, he grants, to explain the plural by appeal to the apostle’s own letter (1 John 5:18–20), but he refuses the parallel: “the plural of a letter ought not to be quoted to explain the plural in an historic document.” That said, he will not let the words be treated as a later gloss — “though the words are an addition, they are a contemporaneous addition present in every important MS. and version, and an undoubted part of the original text.” Who the attestors were he leaves open — “Andrew it may be, or Philip, or some of the seventy disciples,” or men of the Ephesian church such as Aristion or John the Presbyter.

Lightfoot offers a third solution, and a linguistic one. At John 19:35 the Evangelist had written “he knoweth that he saith true”; here he changes the person. Lightfoot suspects “an idiotism in the Chaldee and Syriac tongue, to make ‘We know’ and ‘I know’ the same thing,” citing the Targum, which renders the Hebrew “I know” by “we know” at Joshua 2:9 and 1 Samuel 17:28. On that view no second party need be supposed at all. He adds a point drawn from legal usage: in judicial causes “the ocular testimony prevailed,” and “true” said of testimony means not merely accurate but “sure and irrefragable evidence.”

Chrysostom approaches the attestation from the other end, asking why John appeals to himself at all. The other apostles had said “we are witnesses of these things”; John “is only one who appeals to his own testimony, and he does so, because he was the last who wrote.” That, Chrysostom thinks, is also why he so often mentions Christ’s love for him — “to show the motive which led him to write, and to give weight to his history” — since he was present at every event, even at the crucifixion, when Christ committed his mother to him. And he answers any charge of partiality from the contents: one who meant to show his subject off would have omitted the dishonourable parts, whereas John “selected often reproaches and contumelies in preference to other things.”
25:
The Gospel ends by admitting how much it leaves out. The grammatical-historical commentators note that the “many other things” are not what John has recorded but “the signs and wonders… which are neither recorded by him nor the other evangelists” (Gill), beyond the chosen few (compare John 20:30). Wesley observes that the softening “I suppose” — Robertson marking the first-person singular of the author — “shows that St. John wrote this verse,” and Ellicott reports that the textual evidence strongly supports it, though it is absent from the Sinaitic Codex.

Barnes treats the closing clause as a problem in language, and answers it at length. It is “evidently the figure of speech called a hyperbole,” a mode “where the words express more or less than is literally true” — “common among all writers,” and properly used by the sacred writers because, “in recording a revelation to men,” they “used human language.” He is careful that no untruth is involved: the figure “is commonly the effect of surprise, or having the mind full of some object, and not having words to express the ideas,” yet “the words convey no falsehood,” since a statement “is to be taken as it would be understood among the persons to whom it is addressed.” Because nobody takes it literally, “there is no deception in the case, and consequently no impeachment of his veracity or inspiration.”

His illustrations come from outside Scripture and in. Longinus said of a man that “he was the owner of a piece of ground not larger than a Lacedaemonian letter,” and Virgil of another that “he was so tall as to reach the stars” — in neither case was anyone misled; the one meant a very small field and the other a very tall man. So here John “clearly intends nothing more than that a great many books would be required,” or that it would be “extremely difficult to record them all” — intimating “that his life was active, that his discourses were numerous, and that he had not pretended to give them all.” The same figure, Barnes adds, occurs elsewhere in Scripture (Genesis 11:4; 15:5; Numbers 13:33; Daniel 4:20).

Barnes then turns the book itself into an argument. This Gospel “contains in itself the clearest proof of inspiration”: it is “the work of a fisherman of Galilee, without any proof that he had any unusual advantages,” written “many years after the ascension,” and yet it preserves “the record of the Saviour’s profoundest discourses” and “the purest and most elevated views of God to be found anywhere, as far exceeding all the speculations of philosophers as the sun does the blaze of a taper.” To suppose “that an unlettered fisherman could have originated this book” he judges “in the highest degree absurd”; that such a man preserved the record after so long is itself evidence that he wrote under divine guidance, and so a standing proof of the promise that the Spirit would guide the apostles into all truth (John 14:26).

Calvin reads the verse as guarding the narrative from the charge of partiality: John “has passed over more than he has written,” recording what bears on Christ’s public office. Henry draws the devout response — “let us bless God for all that is in the Scriptures, and be thankful that there is so much in so small a space… Enough is recorded to direct our faith and regulate our practice; more would have been unnecessary” — which is the point of the Evangelist’s own stated purpose (John 20:31).
